title: Programming Principles and Paradigms
description: Programming fundamentals and the families of programming languages; imperative, procedural, object-oriented, functional and logic paradigms; criteria for evaluating languages; syntax, BNF and ambiguity; type systems, overloading and casting; control structures, scope and binding; and memory management in programs. Built from the Ibadan Distance Learning course book and lecture slides for CSC 331.

topics.title: Programming Fundamentals and Types of Languages
topics.summary: Programming is writing source code that a compiler or interpreter turns into a meaningful task, at levels from declarative and high-level languages down to assembly and machine code. Languages are grouped by purpose: scientific, business, educational, object-oriented, functional, declarative, scripting and web languages.
subtopics: Meaning of programming and its stakeholders
Four levels of language: declarative, high-level, assembly, machine
Object-oriented, functional, declarative and scripting languages
Strongly, weakly and loosely typed languages

topics.title: Programming Paradigms
topics.summary: A paradigm is a fundamental style of programming: imperative (structured, procedural, modular, object-oriented) says how, while declarative (functional, logic) says what. Functional languages treat functions as first-class values and rest on the lambda calculus.
subtopics: Imperative languages and the von Neumann model

topics.title: Evaluating Programming Languages
topics.summary: Languages are compared on expressivity, well-definedness, data types, modularity, I/O facilities, portability, efficiency, pedagogy and generality. Other design criteria include simplicity, binding, orthogonality, reliability, applicability, abstraction and efficient implementation.
subtopics: Data types, modularity and I/O facilities

topics.title: Syntax, BNF and Ambiguity
topics.summary: Syntax is the set of rules for well-formed programs; semantics gives their meaning. BNF defines syntax with rewriting rules; lexical analysis turns code into tokens and syntax analysis builds a parse tree, where an ambiguous grammar gives two trees.
subtopics: Syntax and semantics; static and dynamic semantics
Lexical categories: identifiers, literals, operators, separators, keywords
The compiling process: lexical, syntactic and semantic analysis
Syntactic ambiguity and the dangling else

topics.title: Type Systems, Overloading and Casting
topics.summary: A type is a set of values with operations on them, and a type system assigns types to program constructs to catch errors statically or dynamically. Overloading gives one name several meanings, and conversion or casting turns a value of one type into another.
subtopics: Types, type systems and type errors
Elementary and structured types and their storage
Static and dynamic, weak and strong typing
Operator overloading in C++ and Java

topics.title: Control Structures, Scope and Binding
topics.summary: Control statements (sequence, selection, iteration, recursion; for, while, do, switch, break, continue) order a program's execution. The scope of a declaration is the statements that can use it; names are hidden by inner declarations, and bindings have a lifetime.
subtopics: Static scope: global, local and nested

topics.title: Memory Management in Programs
topics.summary: At run time a program's memory is divided into a static area, a run-time stack of method frames and a heap for dynamic data. Arguments are passed by value or by reference, and pointers, arrays and structures are stored in these areas.
subtopics: Static memory, the run-time stack and the heap
Stack frames, static and dynamic links
Passing by value and by reference
